dedupe_keys.name: impact of the 2016 philadelphia transit strike on bike share use interrupted time series

description: This study by Daniel Fuller, Hui Luan, Richard Buote and Amy Auchincloss (Journal of Transport and Health, 2019) uses the strike by Philadelphia's transit workers from 1 to 7 November 2016, which stopped all transit services in the city, as a natural experiment on the use of the city's bicycle share programme. Coverage: daily bike share trips in Philadelphia, analysed with interrupted time series and Bayesian structural time series models, overall and by membership type, controlling for daily temperature and precipitation and for bike share use per 100,000 people in Washington, Boston and Chicago. The strike increased use by 86 to 92 trips per 100,000 population on average, about 57%, with members and non-members up by 41 and 49 trips per 100,000; ridership fell back to baseline as soon as transit returned. Format and access: an open access journal article. Licence and cost: free under CC BY-NC-ND. Caveats: a single one-week event in one city; the shift was not sustained. The measured substitution can be used to set how much transit demand bike share absorbs when simulating transit outages and multimodal network resilience. It relates to the London Tube strike study and Capital Bikeshare data in the catalogue.
